content: Eucalyptus globulus, commonly known as the Tasmanian Blue Gum, Southern Blue Gum, or Blue Gum Eucalyptus, is an evergreen tree that is native to Australia. It is one of the most widely cultivated tree species in the region.7 meters in height. The natural range of this species includes Tasmania and southern Victoria, with isolated populations found on King Island, Flinders Island in Bass Strait, and the summit of the You Yangs. The bark of Eucalyptus globulus frequently sheds, peeling off in large strips. These leaves are covered with a blue-grey, waxy coating, which gives the tree its common name, blue gum. In contrast, the mature leaves are narrow, sickle-shaped, and dark green with a glossy appearance. These leaves are alternately arranged on rounded stems and can grow to lengths of 15 to 35 centimeters. The flower buds of the Tasmanian Blue Gum are top-shaped, ribbed, and warty, with a flattened cap (operculum) that features a central knob. The flowers themselves are cream-colored and grow singly in the axils of the leaves. They produce a significant amount of nectar, which is used to create a strongly flavored honey. The fruits of the tree are woody, measuring 1.5 to 2.5 centimeters in diameter, and release numerous small seeds through valves that open at the top of the fruit. The root system of Eucalyptus globulus extends throughout the soil profile, penetrating several feet deep in some soil types. However, the tree does not develop a taproot. On November 27, 1962, the Tasmanian Blue Gum was officially designated as the floral emblem of Tasmania. The species name globulus is derived from the Latin word for little button, referring to the shape of the operculum. Eucalyptus globulus is the most commonly cultivated plantation hardwood in Australia, accounting for 65% of all plantation hardwood in the country. Approximately 4,500 square kilometers of land are dedicated to its cultivation, with the majority of these plantations owned by international paper manufacturers. The tree is also widely grown in other parts of the world for its timber and for the extraction of eucalyptus oil from its leaves. It was introduced to California in the mid-1800s and is now a prominent feature in many parks in San Francisco and throughout the state.
